sections.title: How to use these notes
sections.html:
CA 3: Sunday 8 November 2026 · 40% · covers the ENTIRE course. These notes follow the course outline, from communication to reading.

Priority key

  • ⭐⭐⭐ Core. On the outline, in the slides, and practised in class tasks. Learn definitions, lists and examples.
  • ⭐⭐ Know it. Be able to define and give 2–3 points.
  • ⭐ Skim. Background only.

How Dr Mhindu tests: almost every lecture ended with a case study ("identify the barrier / NVC cue / reading technique, give evidence, explain"). Practise answering in this pattern: name it → quote evidence from the scenario → explain the effect → suggest a fix.

Outline topics that are NOT in your slides. The outline lists some topics that none of your 20 files cover: levels and modes of communication, active vs passive listening, the details of concept maps, outlines and Cornell notes, scholarly vs non-scholarly sources, OPAC and class numbers, note making and citation/referencing, and Module 1 (university learning). I filled these in from standard communication-skills content and marked each one "Not in your slides". If a classmate has notes on them, check those too.

sections.title: What is communication?
sections.html:
• From the Latin communicare = to make common / to share (Pearson, 2008). We try to establish commonness with each other.
  • A dynamic process that includes situational factors and changes in the environment. It is a process of interaction.
  • Communication only happens when the message is decoded AND understood, so there must be common ground (shared language or culture).
  • It should be goal-directed to keep the interaction coherent.
  • Full definition to write in the test: a two-way process in which a message is conveyed in a specific format through an appropriate channel from the sender to the receiver, who may react by giving feedback.

checks.q: Which is the full definition of communication you should write in the test?
o: A two-way process in which a message is conveyed in a specific format through an appropriate channel from the sender to the receiver, who may react by giving feedback
Sending information from one person to another
Talking to a group of people
checks.x: Communication only happens when the message is decoded and understood, and the receiver may give feedback.

checks.q: The word communication comes from the Latin communicare, meaning:
checks.x: We try to establish commonness with each other (Pearson, 2008).

sections.title: Elements of the communication process
sections.html:
Elements = the parts or stages of the process that together decide whether communication succeeds or fails. If one is removed, the process may die. All play an important role.

Element Key points
Sender The initiator or source. Comes up with the idea, encodes it, chooses the channel/medium, sends the message, and decodes the receiver's feedback.
Message The idea or thought to be communicated. "Meanings are in people, not in the message": the receiver interprets it through their frame of mind, background, culture, gender, religion and context.
Encoding Putting the message into a suitable, understandable code for sending. The code can be verbal, non-verbal, written, a diagram, model or picture.
Medium The tool, technology or platform used, e.g. telephone, email, WhatsApp, TV, radio, newspaper.
Channel The route or pathway the message travels, e.g. voice call, text message, video call, face-to-face speech, written text, visual images.
Noise Anything that disturbs the process, distorts the message or stops it reaching its destination. It can be audible or inaudible, e.g. a voice too soft or too loud, poor handwriting, a negative attitude. Knowing about noise helps the sender choose a noise-free channel.
Context The physical, psychological or historical environment of the communication. The same words can mean different things in different situations.
Receiver The destination. Interprets the message, and may give feedback, so they also choose a message and channel and encode. In two-way communication, the receiver does everything the sender does.
Decoding Interpreting the message, attaching meaning to it, making sense of it.
Feedback The receiver's message back to the sender: the receiver becomes the sender. It tells the sender whether the message was received and understood, and it continues or completes the process. Not always needed, e.g. instructions and commands.

Trap: medium vs channel. WhatsApp is the medium (platform); a text message or voice note is the channel (pathway).

"Meanings are in people" exercise (the class scenarios): "Your assignment needs more work", Sarah's "Fine." text, and "See me after class". The same words get different meanings because each receiver decodes through their own perception, past experience, emotions and context. A one-word text has no NVC (no tone or face), so the receiver fills the gap with their own assumptions.

checks.q: A student sends a voice note on WhatsApp. What is WhatsApp here?
checks.x: Medium = the platform or tool (WhatsApp). Channel = the pathway (the voice note).

checks.q: Which element is the receiver's message back to the sender?
checks.x: In feedback the receiver becomes the sender. It is not always needed, e.g. commands.

checks.q: "Meanings are in people, not in the message" means that:
o: each receiver interprets a message through their own background, culture and context
only the sender decides the meaning
written messages are clearer than spoken ones
checks.x: The same words get different meanings because each receiver decodes them through their own perception.

sections.title: Principles of communication: the 7 Cs
sections.html:
Memory aid: "3 Cs of content, 2 Cs of shape, 2 Cs of manners": Complete, Correct, Concrete · Concise, Clear · Considerate, Courteous.

C Meaning Example that BREAKS it
Completeness Has all the necessary information. Incomplete messages leave the receiver confused about what to do "We will meet at 3 PM." (no date, venue or agenda)
Correctness Accurate, truthful and free of errors "Botswana was colonised by the French and gained its independence in 1950." (it was a British protectorate; independence was 1966)
Concreteness Specific and tangible, not abstract "The new product is going to be amazing and will change everything."
Conciseness Brief and to the point "I wanted to talk to you about the meeting we had last week, and I just wanted to say that it was really great, and…" (long and repetitive)
Clarity Clear and easy to understand: simple, direct language. If unclear, the receiver should seek clarification "The new policy will be implemented soon, and it will affect many things."
Consideration Sensitive to the audience's needs and feelings "You are always careless with the handling of apparatus!"
Courtesy Polite and respectful "Do this now, or else!"
  • If these are missing, they create barriers and make communication ineffective.
  • The message should also have a logical flow to achieve coherence. The barriers slide lists coherence among the Cs (and leaves out consideration), so if a question says "coherence", accept it as one of the Cs.

checks.q: "We will meet at 3 PM." (no date, venue or agenda) breaks which of the 7 Cs?
checks.x: It leaves out necessary information.

checks.q: "Do this now, or else!" breaks which C?
checks.x: It is not polite or respectful.

checks.q: Which three Cs are the Cs of content in the memory aid?
checks.x: 3 Cs of content (Complete, Correct, Concrete), 2 of shape (Concise, Clear), 2 of manners (Considerate, Courteous).

sections.title: Levels and modes of communication
sections.html:
The outline lists these under Module 2, so expect at least a short question.

Levels of communication

  • Intrapersonal: communication within yourself: thinking, self-talk, planning, reflecting. Example: deciding how to study for this test.
  • Interpersonal: between two people (or a few), usually face to face. Example: asking a lecturer a question after class.
  • Group (small group): about 3 to 12 people working towards a shared goal. Example: a tutorial group preparing a presentation.
  • Public: one speaker to a large audience. Example: a lecture or speech.
  • Mass: through mass media to a huge, scattered audience. Example: radio, TV, newspapers.

Modes of communication in academic contexts (the outline's examples)

  • Oral: spoken, e.g. lectures, tutorials, presentations, discussions.
  • Written: e.g. tests, assignments, lab reports, emails.
  • Computer-mediated communication (CMC): communication through computers or networks, e.g. e-Learning / Moodle, discussion forums, email, Teams, WhatsApp groups.

Verbal vs non-verbal

  • Verbal = uses words, spoken or written.
  • Non-verbal = without words: body language, tone, space and so on (see Part 2).

checks.q: Deciding on your own how to study for a test is which level of communication?
checks.x: Intrapersonal = communication within yourself.

checks.q: Moodle forums, email and WhatsApp groups are examples of:
checks.x: CMC = communication through computers or networks.

sections.title: Barriers to effective communication
sections.html:
Definition: "any factor or situation that interferes with the communication process and prevents it from being successful" (Conradie et al., 2000:46). Also: "any factor which hampers or prevents the smooth flow of information from the sender to the receiver" (Carey, 2010:11). In short: breakdowns and distortions in the communication process.

A) Barriers caused by the sender and receiver

  1. Differing perceptions (perceptual barriers). Perception = how we see things, our worldview. Caused by differences in language, background, education, past experience, intelligence, occupation and jargon, interests, needs, personality, age, gender, culture, religion and emotional well-being. Also technological barriers: not knowing how to use the devices.
  2. Attitude and stereotyping.
    • Attitude: our tendency to respond in a certain way. If you despise the sender, you won't take the message seriously.
    • Stereotyping: "painting a group with the same brush", judging people by previously formed opinions that may be untrue.
  3. Poor encoding. The sender fails to put the message in an understandable form: wrong vocabulary or language, poor grammar, spelling or punctuation, ambiguity.
  4. Poor decoding. The receiver attaches the wrong meaning, e.g. "If the child does not like the milk, boil it" (boil the child or the milk?).
  5. Lack of feedback. The sender doesn't know if the message was understood, or is too busy sending to notice the feedback.
  6. Poor choice of medium or channel. It delays the message or stops it arriving.
  7. Poor timing. The receiver isn't ready, e.g. announcing a wedding at a funeral.
  8. Perfunctory or marginal attention. Half-listening: forming your reply, wandering thoughts, chatting on social media.
  9. Hoarding and omission.
    • Hoarding = sitting on information to feel powerful (gatekeeping).
    • Omission = deleting parts of a message as it is passed on, e.g. middle managers watering down messages going up a bureaucracy.
  10. Information overload. Too much information, so the receiver is confused.

B) Barriers caused by external factors

  • Physical: environmental noise, mountains, bad weather, technological failure, distance.
  • Bureaucracy: delays the message.
  • Size of audience: e.g. a mass lecture.

Overcoming barriers

  • Choose the right medium, and communicate with the right person.
  • Be concise but complete: not too little and not too much.
  • Be clear: avoid ambiguity.
  • Time your message.
  • Use the right language: avoid idioms.
  • Give feedback.
  • Be culturally sensitive and avoid emotional distress.
  • Follow the 7 Cs.

Tutorial case study: the water-quality lab (Dr Molapisi)

Practise this; a scenario like it is very likely. Model answer:

☐ Barrier (type) Evidence Effect Fix
Technological / physical (external) Internet down in residences, so the email was missed Some students never got the instructions Send instructions earlier and through several channels; brief everyone at the start of the practical
Physical noise (external) Loud construction near the lab Couldn't hear the explanations Close doors or move venue; use a microphone and give written steps
Perceptual / language barrier Students from different backgrounds read scientific terms differently Misunderstood the procedure Give a glossary of key terms; check understanding
Fear of judgement / lack of feedback International students afraid to ask because of their accents Confusion went uncorrected Create a safe Q&A space; allow anonymous questions
Information overload Lecturer, manuals, slides, WhatsApp and LMS all at once Confusion, so the wrong samples were collected Use one official source of instructions
Emotional / psychological (attitude) Kaone's anxiety from the last test means poor attention (marginal attention) Missed instructions Encouragement; support from the lecturer or counsellor
Attitude / perception of the sender Letso believes the lecturer favours top students, so ignores the guidance Rejected the message Fair, open communication from the lecturer

Q3 (greatest impact): information overload is a strong choice, because it directly caused the wrong samples to be collected and it affected everyone, not one student. Justify whichever you choose with evidence from the case.

checks.q: A lecturer uses heavy technical jargon with first-years. Which barrier is this?
checks.x: The sender fails to put the message in a form the receiver understands.

checks.q: Announcing a wedding at a funeral is an example of:
checks.x: The receiver is not ready for the message.

checks.q: Middle managers water down a message as it moves up the organisation. This barrier is:
checks.x: Omission = deleting parts of a message as it is passed on.

sections.title: What is NVC?
sections.html:
• "Information that is communicated without using words" (Hybels and Weaver II, 2004:170).
  • "Communication consisting of symbols that are not words, including non-word vocalisations" (Pearson et al., 2003:107).
  • "Messages expressed without words" (Galvin, Cooper and Gordon, 1994:24).

Key facts

  • NVC is harder to fake than words: "actions speak louder than words".
  • About two-thirds of all communication is non-verbal.
  • NVC is culture-bound and ambiguous: it has no fixed meaning and can be read in different ways.

checks.q: About how much of all communication is non-verbal?
checks.x: About two-thirds of communication is non-verbal.

checks.q: Why is NVC hard to interpret?
o: It always means the same thing
checks.x: NVC has no fixed meaning and can be read in different ways.

sections.title: Types of NVC cues
sections.html:
Type What it covers Example or warning
Kinesics (body language) Posture, body movement, gestures, facial expressions, eye contact Leaning forward vs back; fidgeting, tapping feet; nodding, pointing, waving; smiling, frowning, winking
Oculesics Eye contact (part of kinesics) Direct gaze, eye avoidance
Proxemics Space and distance: intimate, personal, social, public A CEO seated far from staff may suggest authoritarian leadership. Students sitting close aren't necessarily lovers, so it can be misread
Chronemics (temporal) Use of time: punctuality, lateness, time spent with someone or on a task Arriving late to a meeting may say "this isn't important to me"
Haptics (tactile) Touch Warmth, consoling, welcoming, sealing a deal. Rules differ across cultures (Pearson et al., 2003)
Paralanguage (paralinguistics, vocalics) How words are said: tone, volume, speed, pitch. Non-word sounds: ah, eh, eish, umm, wooow. Silence Silence can mean agreement, disagreement, fear, shyness, respect, anger, confusion, concentration…
Dressing (clothing, adornment, jewellery) Culture, religion, occupation, status, occasion Can mislead: black doesn't always mean mourning
Olfactics Smell, e.g. perfume Can be misinterpreted
Body appearance Tall, short, thin, fat Linked to personality traits, often wrongly

checks.q: Arriving late to a meeting communicates through:
checks.x: Chronemics = the use of time.

checks.q: Touch as non-verbal communication is called:
checks.x: Haptics (tactile).

checks.q: Tone, volume, pitch, "umm" and silence belong to:
checks.x: Paralanguage is how words are said, plus non-word sounds and silence.

sections.title: Functions of NVC
sections.html:
Memory aid: "RCS-CREA": Repeat, Complement, Substitute, Contradict, Regulate, Express emotion, Accent.

  1. Repeating: "Head to the right" while pointing right.
  2. Complementing: smiling while saying "I'm so glad to see you".
  3. Substituting: replaces the words, e.g. a nod for "yes", a shrug for "I don't know", a wave to greet.
  4. Contradicting: "I'm fine" in a flat tone.
  5. Regulating the conversation: raising a finger to speak, breaking eye contact to wrap up.
  6. Expressing emotion and relationships: leaning forward shows engagement; a tall posture asserts authority.
  7. Accenting (emphasising): hand gestures to stress a point.

checks.q: Saying "I'm fine" in a flat tone is NVC that:
checks.x: The tone contradicts the words.

checks.q: A nod in place of saying "yes" is NVC that:
checks.x: It replaces the words.

checks.q: Raising a finger to show you want to speak is NVC that:
checks.x: It manages turn-taking.

sections.title: NVC class case study: the water purification project
sections.html:
Cue Who Appeared to mean Function
Eye contact and hand gestures while explaining Kaone Confidence; illustrating steps Complementing / accenting
Frequent nodding Tshenolo Agreement, attention Regulating / complementing (encourages the speaker)
Arms folded, rarely looks at the speaker, leans back, looks at the clock Mpho Boredom, disinterest (misread)
Smile and thumbs-up Laone Approval of Tshenolo's idea Substituting ("good idea")
Eye-rolling and a loud sigh Mpho Dismissal, irritation Expressing emotion; it silenced Tshenolo
Leans forward, takes notes Laone Engagement Expressing relational dynamics
Everyone sits upright when the lecturer passes Group Respect, wanting to look serious Regulating / expressing relationships (status)

The misunderstood cue: Mpho's folded arms and clock-watching. Kaone read them as boredom, but Mpho was cold and worried about his next class.

Lesson (the limitation of NVC): NVC is ambiguous and context-dependent. Check the meaning (ask, or look for verbal confirmation) before you conclude. Real-life example: avoiding eye contact may be respect in Setswana culture but read as dishonesty in another culture.

checks.q: In the water purification case, what did Mpho's folded arms and clock-watching really mean?
o: He was cold and worried about his next class
checks.x: Kaone read them as boredom. The lesson: NVC is ambiguous, so check the meaning before concluding.

sections.title: Listening
sections.html:
Definition: listening is hearing with a purpose, the art of hearing and understanding what someone says, so that the brain absorbs the meaning of words and sentences.

"The ability to listen and understand is the most important skill for an effective and successful student" (Erasmus-Kritzinger et al., 2007).

Listening is an active process of concentrating, absorbing, interpreting, judging, visualising, trying to understand, and acting on what you hear.

Listening Hearing
Active process Passive process
Requires concentration No concentration
Leads to interpretation No interpretation
You try to understand No understanding needed
You act on what you hear No action required

Active vs passive listening

  • Active listening: fully engaged. You concentrate, take notes, ask questions, give feedback (nods, eye contact) and think about the meaning.
  • Passive listening: you just let the sound in, with no effort to understand, question or respond. Hearing, not listening.

The 3 As of active listening

  1. Attitude. Keep a positive, constructive attitude, which leads to open-mindedness. Don't assume a lecture will be dull. Don't conclude the lecturer is wrong just because you disagree.
  2. Attention. Focus on the lecture, so that the ideas are actually processed.
  3. Adjustment. Be flexible: follow the lecture wherever it goes, and ask questions for clarity.

Class task (outcome if a factor is ignored): without attention you miss key points and your notes have gaps. With a negative attitude you reject useful information. Without adjustment you get lost when the lecturer digresses.

Poor listening habits

  • Criticising the speaker; finding fault with the speaker.
  • Letting yourself be distracted; faking attention.
  • Comparing lecturers.
  • Listening only for facts; listening only to the easy material.
  • Calling a subject boring.
  • Overreacting to emotional words.

Challenges of listening in academic contexts

  • Lecturers speak too fast (they need to cover the syllabus).
  • Information overload; forgetting what was taught.
  • Complex information and unfamiliar words; disorganised lectures and digressions.
  • Unfamiliar accents; noisy lecture rooms.
  • Lack of concentration, lack of interest, or dislike of the lecturer.
  • Long hours in the lecture room.

Recognising NVC during lectures

Why observe it? Lecturers' NVC signals emphasis, attitude, engagement, transitions and important information. Watch for when they slow down, point, repeat gestures or change tone.

Lecturer's cue Likely meaning
Leaning forward Emphasis
Raised finger Key point
Pause Important idea
Direct eye contact Engagement; checking understanding
Nodding Agreement or reinforcement
Raised eyebrows Surprise; highlighting a question
Smile Encouragement

Be careful interpreting: the meaning depends on context, culture, situation and the individual.

Dr Molefe case study (photosynthesis): smiles and makes eye contact (welcoming, engaging) · slows her speech (importance) · raises her index finger (key point) · writes key terms on the board · pauses before "This is the concept you must remember for the examination" (the strongest cue for note-taking) · tilts her head and moves closer to confused students (concern, checking understanding).

Conclusion: effective listeners observe as well as hear.

checks.q: Listening differs from hearing because listening is:
o: active, with concentration, interpretation and action
checks.x: Hearing is passive; listening is hearing with a purpose.

checks.q: Which is one of the 3 As of active listening?
checks.x: The 3 As: Attitude, Attention, Adjustment.

checks.q: A lecturer pauses before saying "This is the concept you must remember for the examination". The pause most likely signals:
checks.x: A pause is a strong cue for note-taking.

sections.title: Discourse markers vs signposts
sections.html:
Active listening helps you recognise both of these.

Discourse markers Signposts
What Words or phrases that connect ideas and show the relationships between parts of speech or text Explicit cues that guide the listener through the structure of a talk or text
Purpose (a) link ideas logically; (b) show cause and effect, contrast, sequence; (c) manage turn-taking and tone (a) structure information clearly; (b) help the audience follow the flow; (c) highlight important points, transitions and conclusions
Where Spoken AND written; formal or informal Especially presentations, lectures and academic talks
Examples However (contrast), Therefore (result), In addition (adding), For example (illustration), On the other hand (alternative view), Because, Well, So, Anyway, Actually, By the way "Let's begin with…", "First, let us examine…", "Now let's move on to…", "The key point to remember is…", "To summarise…", "Finally…"

The relationship (a favourite question): signposts are a special type of discourse marker that help an audience navigate a talk. In "First, verbal communication. Next, NVC. Finally, barriers", the words first, next, finally are both. So some signposts are discourse markers, but not all discourse markers are signposts: "however" links ideas but doesn't show where you are in the talk.

Memory aid: discourse markers are connectors; signposts are road signs showing where the speaker is in the talk.

Why notice signposts in lectures? They help you see how ideas are organised, spot what is likely to be examined, decide what to write and how to organise your notes, predict what comes next, and tell main ideas from supporting details.

Class task (social media talk), answer key

  • Signposts: Today, I will discuss (introduces the topic) · To begin with (first point) · Next, I will look at (transition) · Having discussed the challenges, let us consider (transition and recap) · Finally, I will summarise (last section) · In conclusion (conclusion).
  • Discourse markers: For example, An example is (illustration) · In addition, Additionally (adding) · the positives being… the negatives being (contrast).

checks.q: Which of these is a signpost rather than only a discourse marker?
checks.x: Signposts show where the speaker is in the talk; "however" only links ideas.

checks.q: "Therefore" is a discourse marker that shows:
checks.x: Therefore = result or conclusion.

checks.q: Which statement is true?
o: Some signposts are discourse markers, but not all discourse markers are signposts
Signposts are only used in writing
Discourse markers show the structure of a talk
Signposts and discourse markers are exactly the same
checks.x: First, next and finally can be both; however links ideas but is not a signpost.

sections.title: Note-taking from oral sources
sections.html:
Note-TAKING = from oral sources (lectures, tutorials, presentations, audio/video). Note-MAKING = from written sources (Part 6). Don't mix them up.

Why take notes?

  • A record of the lecture.
  • Helps you learn and remember ideas and facts.
  • The basis for integrating all your course materials.
  • Reduces cramming.
  • Shows your understanding of the content.
  • Encourages active thinking in the lecture and further reading.

Effective note-taking: before, during, after

Purpose of note-taking: aids comprehension and retention, outlines the important points, clarifies ideas, and is a source for review.

Before the lecture During After
Review and edit previous notes Listen, think, write Edit soon: the sooner, the less you forget
Think about what's coming next Have a system for taking notes Reorganise
Check the course outline for topics Watch verbal, visual and postural cues: voice inflection, the board, repetition, gestures, slowing down Number, label or underline major and minor points
Turn the topics into questions to answer in class Ask, or write down questions when unsure Remove repetition and irrelevant points
Read or skim the text: new terms, unclear material, gaps Sit in front if you struggle to concentrate Add or clarify; code the margins with key topics
Keep eye contact with the lecturer Reduce the notes; rewrite, outline, map

Note-taking TECHNIQUES (the group tasks)

The details below are from standard study-skills content (Not in your slides).

Technique What it is Layout + Advantages − Disadvantages
Mind mapping (Tony Buzan, 1970s) Ideas organised around ONE central topic, branching outward like a tree, keywords only, colours, symbols Topic in the centre → main branches → sub-branches Whole topic on one page; shows links; easy to remember; quick Gets messy with lots of information; too little detail; hard for others to read
Concept mapping (Joseph Novak) Several concepts in boxes or circles joined by labelled arrows ("causes", "leads to", "is part of"). More like a network, often top-down Main concept at the top → linked concepts with linking words on the arrows Shows relationships clearly; deep understanding; good for science processes Slow to draw; hard during a fast lecture; can get complicated
Outline method Hierarchical: main points on the left, sub-points indented beneath, with numbers or letters (I, A, 1, a) I. Main topic / A. Sub-point / 1. Detail Organised; shows the hierarchy; easy to review and turn into questions Hard if the lecture is disorganised or jumps around; doesn't show links between ideas well
Cornell method (Walter Pauk, Cornell University) The page is split into 3 parts: cue column (left, about 1/3), notes column (right, about 2/3), summary (bottom) Notes during the lecture → keywords or questions in the cue column after → summary at the bottom Built-in revision and self-testing; encourages review Needs page preparation; takes time after class
Digital note-taking Notes typed on a device: OneNote, Word, Google Docs, tablets Headings, colours, links, images, audio Searchable, editable, easy to share and back up, multimedia Distractions (social media); needs power and a device; typing can become word-for-word copying; tech failure

Note-taking STRATEGIES

Abbreviations and symbols: shortcuts that save time.

  • Symbols: → (leads to), = (means), + (and), ↑ (increase), ↓ (decrease), ≠ (not equal), ∴ (therefore), ∵ (because).
  • Abbreviations: e.g. (example), i.e. (that is), b/c (because), w/ (with), w/o (without), approx., govt.
  • Downside: you may forget what your own abbreviations meant.

Short phrases and keywords: write only the words that carry the meaning, not full sentences.

  • Lecturer: "RAM, which stands for random access memory, is a type of primary storage that is volatile, meaning that everything stored in it is lost when the computer is switched off."
  • Notes: RAM = primary storage, volatile → data lost when off
  • + Fast; you listen more; you focus on main ideas; short notes for revision.
  • − Meaning can be lost later; you may pick the wrong keywords; not good for exact definitions or formulas.

Tip: review and expand keyword notes within 24 hours.

checks.q: Notes from a lecture are called:
checks.x: Note-TAKING = oral sources. Note-MAKING = written sources.

checks.q: Which note-taking technique splits the page into a cue column, a notes column and a summary?
checks.x: Walter Pauk's Cornell method; it has built-in self-testing.

checks.q: Ideas branching outward from ONE central topic with keywords and colours is:
checks.x: Mind mapping (Tony Buzan). Concept maps join several concepts with labelled arrows.

sections.title: Oral communication
sections.html:
Definition: the use of spoken language to convey a message. It is the primary means of communication, with four elements: sender, medium, message, receiver.

Academic oral contexts: class discussions, conversations with lecturers, speeches, phone calls, class presentations, lectures, seminars and tutorials, group discussions and debates, oral exams and defences, conferences and symposia.

Oral communication skills: active listening, questioning, using NVC, clarifying, reinforcing.

Advantages Disadvantages
One-on-one contact Can't be received in absentia (you must be there)
Room for further probing No permanent record (unless minutes are taken)
You can use and read NVC Open to barriers: stereotyping, background noise
Both sides take part, with instant feedback Time-consuming if debate is allowed
No distortion of facts one-on-one Inaccessible to people with hearing impairments
Reaches a large audience at once Sensitive information may be shared inappropriately; misread across cultures; information overload

Solutions to the disadvantages: visual aids, written summaries at the end, recording, watching the audience's reactions.

checks.q: Which is a disadvantage of oral communication?
o: There is no permanent record unless minutes are taken
It reaches a large audience at once
checks.x: The others are advantages.

sections.title: Types of speech delivery
sections.html:
Type What it is Best for + −
Extemporaneous Planned, researched and practised, but delivered from brief notes or an outline, not a script Lectures, keynotes, business presentations, most formal speaking Natural, flexible, eye contact, adapts to the audience Needs lots of preparation; may forget wording or exact figures
Impromptu On the spot, little or no preparation Q&A, unexpected updates, sudden requests Authentic, spontaneous Needs quick thinking and strong mental organisation
Manuscript Read word for word from a text or teleprompter (autocue) Press conferences, government addresses, legal statements Complete accuracy, precise timing, nothing forgotten Little eye contact; sounds flat or robotic; hard to adapt to the audience
Memorised Written word for word, then memorised, no notes Short ceremonial speeches, elevator pitches, competitions Total eye contact, free movement Memory lapses; sounds robotic

Class question (presenting a science experiment): choose extemporaneous. It is well prepared, so it is accurate, but notes let you check figures while still keeping eye contact and answering questions.

Beating stage fright: rehearse, know your material, breathe slowly, arrive early to check the venue, focus on the message rather than yourself, start with a prepared opening, make eye contact with friendly faces.

checks.q: A speech planned and practised but delivered from brief notes is:
checks.x: Extemporaneous: natural, flexible, keeps eye contact.

checks.q: Which delivery type is best for a press conference or legal statement?
checks.x: Manuscript gives complete accuracy and precise timing.

checks.q: Which type of delivery should you choose to present a science experiment, according to the class question?
checks.x: Well prepared and accurate, with notes for figures, while still keeping eye contact.

sections.title: Preparing an oral presentation
sections.html:
Three stages: (1) Planning (occasion, audience, purpose, thesis, material) → (2) Outlining and structuring (intro, body, conclusion) → (3) Choosing the mode of delivery.

Research: content must be authentic and supported by evidence from credible sources.

Audience analysis (know all 10): socio-political or economic background · age · gender · level of education · cultural background · language · status · population (size). Example: level of education decides how much jargon you can use.

Also plan timing, venue and rehearsal (from the outline).

The outline: a framework into which the pieces of your material fit. It guides you and keeps the presentation orderly. Good structure makes the message clearer, creates the desired effect, and boosts your image as a speaker.

Introduction Main body Conclusion
Grab attention · introduce the topic · preview the speech · set the rules for questions · smooth transition All main points and supporting material, in a logical sequence Summary · closing statement or re-emphasis · vote of thanks · invitation to questions

Audio-visual aids (slides, videos, images, audio, posters):

  • Benefits: more confidence, better organisation, better engagement, less nervousness.
  • Rules: (1) keep them simple and concise; (2) practise with them; (3) check they work with the equipment; (4) use high-quality visuals and audio.

Class task (water pollution plan), rearranged

  • Introduction: picture of a polluted river (grabs attention).
  • Body: causes of pollution (diagram) → water quality tests (table of results) → fish deaths (a simple graph or video).
  • Conclusion: solutions (bullet list or image).
  • Don't start with a complex graph: it confuses the audience before they have context.

checks.q: What are the three stages of preparing an oral presentation?
o: Planning → outlining and structuring → choosing the mode of delivery
checks.x: Planning, then outlining, then the mode of delivery.

checks.q: Which belongs in the conclusion of a presentation?
o: A summary and a vote of thanks
checks.x: The conclusion summarises, re-emphasises, thanks and invites questions.

sections.title: Delivering an oral presentation
sections.html:
DO DON'T
Use clear, concise language Read from the slides or notes (disengages the audience, lowers credibility)
Keep eye contact (connection, confidence) Speak too fast (overwhelms) or too slowly (loses attention); aim for a moderate pace with pauses
Use visual aids; use slides as prompts and speak naturally Use jargon the audience doesn't know
Engage the audience: questions, stories, real examples Ignore the time limit
Manage your voice: vary tone, pace and volume; pause for emphasis Ignore audience feedback (body language, questions)
NVC: stand confidently, gesture naturally
Handle questions gracefully: listen, answer respectfully, admit when you don't know, offer to follow up
Manage time: stick to it; prioritise key points

End with a clear summary and a memorable closing statement.

Giving and receiving feedback (Q&A)

  • Receiving: listen fully, thank the person, don't get defensive.
  • Giving: be specific and polite; start with a strength, then one improvement.

Activity answer (the bad lab presenter)

Mistake Why it hurts Fix
Reads slides word for word Boring; looks unprepared Use keywords as prompts
Avoids eye contact No connection; looks nervous Look around the room
Speaks too softly The audience can't hear Project the voice
Turns their back to the audience Loses attention; voice lost Face the audience; stand beside the screen
Too much text on the slides Information overload Short bullets, visuals

checks.q: When you don't know the answer to a question after your presentation, you should:
o: admit it and offer to follow up
checks.x: Handle questions gracefully: listen, answer respectfully, admit when you don't know.

checks.q: Too much text on the slides causes:
checks.x: Use short bullets and visuals instead.

sections.title: Information sources
sections.html:
Definition: an information source is any place, person, document or resource from which we get information or evidence to understand, investigate or answer a question.

Steps to identify a relevant source

  1. Identify what information you need.
  2. Find appropriate sources.
  3. Evaluate reliability and relevance.
  4. Use the information appropriately.
  5. Cite the source.

Matching the source to the information need

Source Gives you
Journal article Findings from academic research
Book Detailed discussion of a subject
Statistical report Numbers, e.g. Statistics Botswana
Newspaper article Recent events or issues
Government report Official information and statistics
Law or Act The actual legal rules, e.g. Data Protection Act (2024), Cybercrime and Computer-Related Crimes Act (2018)
Encyclopaedia Overview or background
Interview Information from a person with knowledge or experience
Survey Information from a group of people
Thesis or dissertation Original research using many sources

Class assignment ("How does social media influence young people in Botswana?")

  • Journal articles (psychological and social effects).
  • Statistics Botswana (usage figures).
  • Data Protection Act and Cybercrime Act (legal).
  • Newspapers (recent cases).
  • Survey or interviews with students (first-hand).

Primary, secondary and tertiary

Type Definition Examples
Primary Original, first-hand information; direct evidence; reports a discovery or new information Diaries, letters, autobiographies, research articles, interviews, survey data, experiment results, the Constitution or Acts, court judgments, speeches, census data, photos
Secondary Created by someone who did not experience it first-hand; analyses, interprets or discusses primary sources; one or more steps removed Textbooks, review articles, histories, criticisms, commentaries
Tertiary Collect, organise and summarise primary and secondary sources for a general overview Encyclopaedias, handbooks, dictionaries, reference sources

Trap: your slides list encyclopaedias under secondary in one place and tertiary in another. If asked, call an encyclopaedia tertiary (a summary or overview).

Scholarly vs non-scholarly

Scholarly (journals) Non-scholarly (popular: magazines, newspapers, blogs, social media)
Reports original research and in-depth analysis General interest, news, entertainment
Written by scholars or researchers (credentials given) Journalists, staff writers, anyone; author often missing
Audience: scholars, researchers, students Audience: the general public
Scholarly language and jargon Simple, everyday language
Usually peer-reviewed Edited by staff or not reviewed at all
Full documentation of sources (references) Few or no references
E.g. Journal of Personality, JAMA E.g. Mmegi, Time, Wikipedia

Peer review = experts in the field check the article before it is published.

Formal vs informal sources (Not in your slides):

  • Formal: published and controlled sources, e.g. books, journals, reports, databases.
  • Informal: people and unpublished material, e.g. conversations, lecturers, colleagues, social media posts, personal blogs.

Organisation of information and searching

  • Class number: a call number (e.g. Dewey Decimal or Library of Congress) that groups books by subject, so books on the same subject sit together on the shelves (physical arrangement).
  • OPAC = Online Public Access Catalogue: the library's searchable catalogue. Search by author, title, subject or keyword to find a book's class number and location.
  • Databases (e.g. EBSCOhost, ScienceDirect, JSTOR through the UB Library): collections of journal articles you search online.
  • The search process: define the topic → pick keywords and synonyms → combine them with AND / OR / NOT → search the OPAC or databases → evaluate the results → locate and retrieve → cite.

Human sources: librarians (including subject librarians), library service desks, lecturers, colleagues.

checks.q: A student needs the percentage of Batswana aged 18–35 who use the internet. Best source?
checks.x: Numbers come from a statistical report.

checks.q: A research article reporting new findings is a:
checks.x: It reports first-hand, original research.

checks.q: A textbook is usually a:
checks.x: It analyses and interprets others' work.

sections.title: Social media and professionalism
sections.html:
Social media: internet-based platforms that let users create, share and interact with user-generated content while building networks and online communities. They work in real time and are used for professional, personal and marketing purposes.

Kaplan and Haenlein (2010): internet-based platforms using Web 2.0 technologies for the creation, sharing and exchange of user-generated content, letting people and organisations network, collaborate and form online communities.

5 characteristics (memory aid "POCCC"):

  • Participation: users contribute, not just consume.
  • Openness: sharing, feedback, interaction.
  • Conversation: communication flows in many directions, unlike traditional media.
  • Community: groups form around shared interests.
  • Connectedness: linked by hyperlinks, tags, follows and shares.

Examples: Facebook, YouTube, LinkedIn (professional), TikTok, X/Twitter, Instagram, WhatsApp.

Key terms

  • Digital professionalism (e-professionalism): showing professional values, behaviour, ethics, competence and accountability when using digital technology and social media. A new paradigm that needs training, codes and practices.
    • The Australian Medical Association (2020) and the Health Professions Council of South Africa (2019) advise against doctor–patient friendships on social media. HPCSA: even personal or anonymous use must follow the code of conduct.
    • Rose and Mishnick (2025): found unprofessional online behaviour among trainee teachers and recommend teaching digital professionalism.
  • Digital footprint: the cumulative record of data from your use of websites, social media, apps and devices. It includes both intentionally shared and automatically collected data, and it reaches beyond your immediate contacts.
  • Online identity: your digital representation, built from your activities, profiles and footprint. It includes how you present yourself and how others see you.
    • Components: personal identity, professional identity, social media presence, academic identity, reputation and credibility.
  • Personal vs professional use: the line is blurred, because the same platforms are used for both. Employers screen applicants using social media footprints (Rose and Mishnick, 2025; Melanthiou and Pavlou, 2015).
  • Confidentiality cases:
    • Mark Small: a lawyer rebuked for gloating online about a case win.
    • Penny Sparrow: racist Facebook post; personal posts with professional consequences.

Information disorder

The internet caused information overload, which led to information disorder: sharing or creating false (or harmful) information, with or without intent to harm.

Type Formula Example
Misinformation Wrong information + no intent to harm Sharing "hot water, honey and garlic cures COVID-19" because you believe it; the AI image of the Pope in a puffer jacket
Disinformation Wrong / fabricated + intent to harm or scam Fake video of "President Boko" promoting an investment scheme to Batswana
Malinformation TRUE information + intent to harm Leaking confidential patient records; #GuptaLeaks (2017, genuine emails); WikiLeaks / Julian Assange

Memory aid: Mis = Mistake, Dis = Deliberate lie, Mal = true but Malicious.

Risks of information disorder

Risk Impact
Poor decision-making Wrong personal and public choices
Reputational damage Loss of credibility and trust
Erosion of trust Less confidence in institutions
Social conflict Polarisation and tension
Democratic harm Manipulated elections and public opinion
Economic losses Financial and business damage
Health risks Unsafe health behaviour
Psychological harm Stress, anxiety, harassment
Cybersecurity threats Fraud, identity theft
National security Instability, unrest
Education Poor learning and research quality

Evaluating content: the CRAAP test

Letter Question
Currency Is it up to date?
Relevance Does it meet my information need?
Authority Who is the author? Their credentials?
Accuracy Is it correct and supported by evidence?
Purpose Why was it created or shared (inform, sell, persuade, harm)?

Protecting personal data

  • Strong passwords; two-factor authentication.
  • Review app permissions.
  • Limit the personal information you share.
  • Update software regularly.
  • Use privacy settings.
  • "Your data has value."

checks.q: Sharing "hot water, honey and garlic cures COVID-19" because you believe it is:
checks.x: Wrong information with no intent to harm.

checks.q: Leaking genuine confidential patient records to cause harm is:
checks.x: Mal = true but malicious.

checks.q: A fake video of a president promoting an investment scam is:
checks.x: Fabricated and meant to harm or scam.

sections.title: What is reading?
sections.html:
• The process of looking at written symbols and getting meaning from them; the conscious process of constructing meaning from written texts.
  • The eyes receive the symbols (letters, punctuation, spaces); the brain turns them into words, sentences and paragraphs.
  • A receptive skill (you take information in). Reading (intake) usually leads to writing (production).
  • Importance: builds general knowledge, spelling, writing and vocabulary; builds the passion to learn; drives success in your courses. If you don't like reading, accept its importance and work on it.

checks.q: Reading is a:
checks.x: You take information in; writing is the productive skill.

sections.title: Purposes for reading
sections.html:
Know why you are reading before you start. The purpose decides the technique.

  • To gain knowledge.
  • To critically analyse evidence.
  • To get general information on a subject.
  • To add to existing knowledge.
  • To propose new ideas.
  • To complete assignments or papers.
  • To prepare for writing or discussion.
  • To solve problems or apply information.

Academic reading contexts: textbooks and scholarly articles, literature reviews for research (identify, compare, synthesise sources), lab reports (methods and results), preparing for lectures.

checks.q: What should decide which reading technique you use?
o: How much time is left in the semester
checks.x: Know why you are reading before you start.

sections.title: Reading vs critical reading
sections.html:
Reading Critical reading
Purpose Grasp the text Make judgements about the text
Activity Understanding Analysing, interpreting, evaluating
Focus What a text says What a text does and means
Questions Information in the text Working, meaning, pattern, evidence, reasoning and assumptions
Direction Within the text Out of the text (links to other knowledge)
Response Summary Description, interpretation and evaluation

Critical-reading task (the homeostasis paragraph), model answers

  • Purpose: explaining how homeostasis works.
  • Sequence: general statement → example (glucose rises, insulin) → opposite case (glucose falls, glucagon) → concept named (negative feedback) → consequence (diabetes).
  • Signal words: For instance, Conversely, These… exemplify.
  • Central idea: homeostasis is kept by negative feedback between the hormone and nervous systems.
  • Implication: if the feedback fails (diabetes), many organs suffer.
  • Terminology: precise, but harder for non-specialists.
  • Convincing? Yes: it has a clear, specific example, though it cites no source.

checks.q: Critical reading differs from reading because it:
o: makes judgements by analysing, interpreting and evaluating
only grasps what the text says
checks.x: Critical reading looks at what a text does and means, and links out to other knowledge.

sections.title: Reading techniques
sections.html:
Academic reading is not casual reading. It needs active engagement, critical thinking and strategy. The purpose decides the technique.

Technique What you do Use it when…
Skimming Read quickly for the general idea (gist). Focus on the first (topic) and last sentences of paragraphs You want to know what a text is about
Scanning Move your eyes quickly to find specific information (a number, name, date, keyword) You need one fact
Intensive reading Deep, slow reading: grammar, unfamiliar words and phrases You must understand every detail
Survey reading (pre-reading) Look at the title, authors, headings, diagrams, tables, abstract, introduction, conclusion and keywords before reading in detail. Helps you predict the content. Saves time Deciding if a text is relevant
Prediction Use the title, headings and pictures to guess what comes next, then read to check Before and during reading (on the outline)
Active reading / annotation Highlight, write in the margins (questions, summaries), underline definitions, circle unfamiliar terms, link to other sources Study reading; it makes revision and note making easier
Critical reading Evaluate arguments and evidence; spot bias and assumptions; compare with other texts Judging the quality of a source
Chunking Break the text into small logical sections, read one, find its main idea, summarise it in your own words, then move on Long or difficult texts
SQ3R Survey → Question → Read → Recite (summarise in your own words) → Review Studying for an exam

Study reading (on the outline) = careful, purposeful reading for learning, combining intensive reading, annotation and note making (SQ3R is a study-reading method).

Trap: skimming vs scanning. Skimming = gist (general). Scanning = specific detail. Memory aid: sCanning = speCific.

Class task: match the scenario to the technique (answers)

  1. Title, abstract, headings, graphs and conclusion to decide relevance → Survey reading.
  2. Highlights findings, circles terms, questions in the margins → Active reading / annotation.
  3. Reads and summarises the Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion separately → Chunking.
  4. Searches the Methods section only for the pH value → Scanning.
  5. Surveys, makes questions, reads, summarises, reviews (malaria) → SQ3R.

checks.q: Looking quickly for the general idea of a text is:
checks.x: Skimming = gist.

checks.q: Searching the Methods section only for the pH value is:
checks.x: sCanning = speCific detail.

checks.q: Survey → Question → Read → Recite → Review is called:
checks.x: SQ3R is a study-reading method.

sections.title: Text-organising features
sections.html:
Texts are organised at book, chapter and paragraph level. Knowing the features helps you read efficiently and selectively: they draw attention to important content and help you anticipate and predict what's coming.

Document navigation (book level)

Feature Purpose
Preface / foreword Explains the book's purpose, organisation and method of presentation
Table of contents Overview or outline of the book and what each chapter covers
Learning objectives What you should be able to do after the chapter
Chapter headings and subheadings Show what each section covers, so you can focus
Review / critical-thinking questions, case studies Help you reflect on what you learnt
Glossary Definitions of technical terms
Index Detailed alphabetical list of topics, with page numbers
Bibliography / reference list Material used in the text; leads to further reading

Structural divisions: headings, subheadings, text boxes, paragraphs (one main idea each, introduced by a topic sentence), abstract (journal articles).

Visual and formatting aids: graphics (tables, charts, graphs, diagrams), bullets, captions and labels, bold or italic text, different fonts and colours.

Trap: glossary vs index. Glossary = meanings of terms. Index = where topics are (page numbers).

Applied to the COVID-19 peer-reviewed article (Naveed et al., 2024, Toxicology Research):

  • Title.
  • Authors with affiliations and a corresponding author.
  • Abstract and key words.
  • Received / revised / accepted dates.
  • Headings (Introduction … Conclusion).
  • Tables (e.g. Table 3, COVID-19 vaccines and their efficiencies) and numbered figures with captions (e.g. Fig. 3, Clinical symptoms).
  • Numbered in-text citations.
  • Author contributions, funding, reference list, DOI.

Most important for readability and credibility

  • The abstract (summary, which allows survey reading).
  • Headings (navigation).
  • References / citations (evidence, which gives credibility).

checks.q: Where do you find the meanings of technical terms in a book?
checks.x: Glossary = meanings. Index = where topics are (page numbers).

checks.q: Which feature of a journal article allows survey reading because it summarises the whole paper?
checks.x: The abstract is the summary.

sections.title: Evaluating sources for reliability
sections.html:
The same idea as CRAAP:

  • Currency: does the topic need current information? Current sources are encouraged.
  • Relevance: does it help answer the question?
  • Authority: who is the author, and what are their credentials?
  • Accuracy / credibility: is it supported by evidence?

Questions to ask

  • What type of source is it, and who wrote it?
  • Is it relevant and specific?
  • Is it academic?
  • Is it biased?
  • What is its purpose?
  • Where did it get its information?
  • Does it support or oppose my conclusion?
  • Are all internet sources reliable? No.
Acceptable (peer-reviewed or edited) NOT acceptable (not reviewed)
Books Wikipedia
Scholarly journal articles ".com" websites
Trade magazines / journals Any source with no identified author or place of publication
Government websites

Use the UB Library databases.

General textbook = secondary source (based on others' work). Journal article = primary source (reports the writer's own empirical research), so it is better for researching a specific topic.

Class task (COVID-19 sources)

  • A blog, Wikipedia or social media post has an unclear author, no peer review, and possible bias or unsupported claims, so don't use it in academic work.
  • The peer-reviewed article has named authors with affiliations, journal peer review, references and a DOI, so it is acceptable.

checks.q: Which source is NOT acceptable for academic work?
checks.x: Wikipedia is not reviewed; the others are peer-reviewed or edited.

sections.title: Reading infographics
sections.html:
An infographic combines images, charts and short text to present data quickly. To read and critique one:

  1. Read the title and source.
  2. Check the axes, units and labels.
  3. Find the main message.
  4. Look for misleading features: cut-off axes, missing source, cherry-picked data.
  5. Apply CRAAP.

sections.title: Note making from written sources, citation and referencing
sections.html:
This is the Week 13 topic and is on the outline. None of your files cover it, so learn the basics below.

Note making = making notes from written texts (books, articles), at your own pace, after reading with SQ3R or chunking. The same techniques as note-taking apply (mind maps, concept maps, outlines, Cornell, digital vs manual), plus these strategies:

Strategy What it means Key rule
Paraphrasing Rewriting one idea or passage in your own words, about the same length Change the words AND the sentence structure; keep the meaning; still cite
Summarising Reducing a text to its main ideas only, in your own words, much shorter Leave out examples and details; still cite
Quoting Copying the author's exact words Use quotation marks + citation (with page number)
Short phrases, abbreviations, symbols Same as note-taking Make sure you can still read them later

Using bibliographic information in note making: at the top of your notes, record the author, year, title, publisher or journal, pages and DOI or URL, so you can cite later and avoid plagiarism.

Plagiarism = presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own without acknowledging them. Copyright = the legal right of the creator over their work. Citation prevents plagiarism and gives credit.

Citation: two parts

  • In-text citation (in the body of your text). APA style:
    • (Naveed et al., 2024), or Naveed et al. (2024) found that…
    • Use et al. for 3 or more authors.
    • Direct quote: add the page, e.g. (Pearson, 2008, p. 5).
  • End-of-text citation = the reference list: full details of every source cited, in alphabetical order by author surname.

Components of a scientific reference (APA journal article)

Author(s) surname, initials. (Year). Title of article. Journal Name, Volume(Issue), pages. DOI

Example from your slides: Kaplan, A. M., & Haenlein, M. (2010). Users of the world, unite! The challenges and opportunities of social media. Business Horizons, 53(1), 59–68. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bushor.2009.09.003

  • Author (who)
  • Year (when)
  • Title (what)
  • Source: journal or publisher (where)
  • Volume, issue and pages
  • DOI or URL

Book (APA): Steinberg, S. (2006). An introduction to communication studies. Juta.

checks.q: Rewriting one idea in your own words at about the same length is:
checks.x: Change the words and the structure, keep the meaning, and still cite.

checks.q: For a source with three or more authors, the in-text citation uses:
o: the first author only, with no marker
checks.x: e.g. (Naveed et al., 2024).

checks.q: Presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own without acknowledging them is:
checks.x: Citation prevents plagiarism and gives credit.

sections.title: Extra: Module 1, university learning
sections.html:
Weeks 1–2 on the outline. CA 3 covers the entire course, so know these basics.

  • Culture of higher education: you are an independent learner. Nobody chases you, and you manage your own reading, deadlines and attendance. Lecturers guide; you do the learning.
  • Goal setting: set SMART goals (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound), both personal and academic.
  • Motivation:
    • Intrinsic = from inside you (interest, enjoying the subject, wanting to understand).
    • Extrinsic = from outside (marks, a bursary, a job, praise, avoiding punishment).
    • Intrinsic motivation usually lasts longer.
  • Learning styles (VARK): Visual (diagrams, mind maps), Auditory (listening, discussion), Reading/writing (notes, texts), Kinaesthetic (doing, labs, practicals). Know yours and study to suit it.
  • Study habits: a regular study place and time, review notes within 24 hours, active methods (self-testing, SQ3R), study groups, avoid cramming.
  • Time management: use a timetable or diary, prioritise (urgent vs important), break big tasks down, avoid procrastination, balance study and rest.
  • Personal organisation: file notes by course, track deadlines, keep a calendar.
  • Class attendance: you get the lecturer's emphasis (NVC, signposts), announcements and notes, and it is often a requirement.
  • Library: orientation and tour; use the OPAC, databases and librarians to reach your learning goals.

sections.title: Last-minute checklist
sections.html:
Can you do each of these without looking? If not, go back to that section.

  • Define communication and explain where the word comes from (communicare).
  • Name and explain the 10 elements. Tell medium from channel.
  • List the 7 Cs and write a sentence that breaks each one.
  • Name the levels (intra, inter, group, public, mass) and modes (oral, written, CMC).
  • Spot 5 barriers in a scenario and give a fix for each.
  • Name the NVC types: kinesics, oculesics, proxemics, chronemics, haptics, paralanguage, olfactics, dress, appearance.
  • Give the 7 functions of NVC with examples.
  • Contrast listening vs hearing. Explain the 3 As and the poor listening habits.
  • Contrast discourse markers vs signposts, and how they relate.
  • Give the importance of notes and before/during/after tips. Describe mind map, concept map, outline, Cornell, digital, with pros and cons.
  • Give the 4 speech delivery types with pros and cons, and which suits a science presentation.
  • List the audience analysis factors. Give the intro/body/conclusion contents and AV-aid rules.
  • List the presentation dos and don'ts.
  • Contrast primary, secondary and tertiary; scholarly vs non-scholarly; match source to need.
  • Define digital professionalism, digital footprint, online identity.
  • Tell mis- / dis- / malinformation apart with examples. Explain CRAAP.
  • Contrast reading vs critical reading. List the purposes of reading.
  • Explain skimming, scanning, survey, chunking, annotation, critical reading, SQ3R, and match scenarios to them.
  • Give the text-organising features and their purposes (glossary vs index).
  • Contrast paraphrase, summary, quote. Explain in-text vs reference list. Name the parts of a reference.

sections.title: Likely question types
sections.html:
1. Define + explain + example (e.g. "Define proxemics and give two examples of how it can be misinterpreted").
  2. Case study: "Identify 5 barriers or NVC cues, quote evidence, explain the effect, suggest a solution."
  3. Match: scenarios → reading techniques, or source → information need.
  4. Distinguish between: listening/hearing, discourse marker/signpost, skimming/scanning, primary/secondary, mis/dis/mal-information, reading/critical reading, note-taking/note-making.
  5. Identify discourse markers and signposts in a short speech.

Good luck tomorrow, Tinashe.

sets.title: CA 3 multiple choice
sets.desc: COM 141 tests are multiple choice. These questions cover every section of the notes, with the reason for each answer.

qs.q: Which is the full definition of communication you should write in the test?
o: A two-way process in which a message is conveyed in a specific format through an appropriate channel from the sender to the receiver, who may react by giving feedback
Sending information from one person to another
Talking to a group of people
qs.x: Communication only happens when the message is decoded and understood, and the receiver may give feedback.

qs.q: The word communication comes from the Latin communicare, meaning:
qs.x: We try to establish commonness with each other (Pearson, 2008).

qs.q: A student sends a voice note on WhatsApp. What is WhatsApp here?
qs.x: Medium = the platform or tool (WhatsApp). Channel = the pathway (the voice note).

qs.q: Which element is the receiver's message back to the sender?
qs.x: In feedback the receiver becomes the sender. It is not always needed, e.g. commands.

qs.q: "Meanings are in people, not in the message" means that:
o: each receiver interprets a message through their own background, culture and context
only the sender decides the meaning
written messages are clearer than spoken ones
qs.x: The same words get different meanings because each receiver decodes them through their own perception.

qs.q: "We will meet at 3 PM." (no date, venue or agenda) breaks which of the 7 Cs?
qs.x: It leaves out necessary information.

qs.q: "Do this now, or else!" breaks which C?
qs.x: It is not polite or respectful.

qs.q: Which three Cs are the Cs of content in the memory aid?
qs.x: 3 Cs of content (Complete, Correct, Concrete), 2 of shape (Concise, Clear), 2 of manners (Considerate, Courteous).

qs.q: Deciding on your own how to study for a test is which level of communication?
qs.x: Intrapersonal = communication within yourself.

qs.q: Moodle forums, email and WhatsApp groups are examples of:
qs.x: CMC = communication through computers or networks.

qs.q: A lecturer uses heavy technical jargon with first-years. Which barrier is this?
qs.x: The sender fails to put the message in a form the receiver understands.

qs.q: Announcing a wedding at a funeral is an example of:
qs.x: The receiver is not ready for the message.

qs.q: Middle managers water down a message as it moves up the organisation. This barrier is:
qs.x: Omission = deleting parts of a message as it is passed on.

qs.q: Sitting on information to feel powerful (gatekeeping) is called:
qs.x: Hoarding.

qs.q: A generator running outside the venue is which kind of barrier?
qs.x: Environmental noise is a physical, external barrier.

qs.q: About how much of all communication is non-verbal?
qs.x: About two-thirds of communication is non-verbal.

qs.q: Why is NVC hard to interpret?
o: It always means the same thing
qs.x: NVC has no fixed meaning and can be read in different ways.

qs.q: Arriving late to a meeting communicates through:
qs.x: Chronemics = the use of time.

qs.q: Touch as non-verbal communication is called:
qs.x: Haptics (tactile).

qs.q: Tone, volume, pitch, "umm" and silence belong to:
qs.x: Paralanguage is how words are said, plus non-word sounds and silence.

qs.q: A CEO seated far from staff may suggest authoritarian leadership. This cue is:
qs.x: Proxemics = use of space and distance.

qs.q: Saying "I'm fine" in a flat tone is NVC that:
qs.x: The tone contradicts the words.

qs.q: A nod in place of saying "yes" is NVC that:
qs.x: It replaces the words.

qs.q: Raising a finger to show you want to speak is NVC that:
qs.x: It manages turn-taking.

qs.q: In the water purification case, what did Mpho's folded arms and clock-watching really mean?
o: He was cold and worried about his next class
qs.x: Kaone read them as boredom. The lesson: NVC is ambiguous, so check the meaning before concluding.

qs.q: Listening differs from hearing because listening is:
o: active, with concentration, interpretation and action
qs.x: Hearing is passive; listening is hearing with a purpose.

qs.q: Which is one of the 3 As of active listening?
qs.x: The 3 As: Attitude, Attention, Adjustment.

qs.q: A lecturer pauses before saying "This is the concept you must remember for the examination". The pause most likely signals:
qs.x: A pause is a strong cue for note-taking.

qs.q: Which of these is a signpost rather than only a discourse marker?
qs.x: Signposts show where the speaker is in the talk; "however" only links ideas.

qs.q: "Therefore" is a discourse marker that shows:
qs.x: Therefore = result or conclusion.

qs.q: Which statement is true?
o: Some signposts are discourse markers, but not all discourse markers are signposts
Signposts are only used in writing
Discourse markers show the structure of a talk
Signposts and discourse markers are exactly the same
qs.x: First, next and finally can be both; however links ideas but is not a signpost.

qs.q: Notes from a lecture are called:
qs.x: Note-TAKING = oral sources. Note-MAKING = written sources.

qs.q: Which note-taking technique splits the page into a cue column, a notes column and a summary?
qs.x: Walter Pauk's Cornell method; it has built-in self-testing.

qs.q: Ideas branching outward from ONE central topic with keywords and colours is:
qs.x: Mind mapping (Tony Buzan). Concept maps join several concepts with labelled arrows.

qs.q: When should you review and expand keyword notes?
qs.x: The sooner you edit, the less you forget.

qs.q: Which is a disadvantage of oral communication?
o: There is no permanent record unless minutes are taken
It reaches a large audience at once
qs.x: The others are advantages.

qs.q: A speech planned and practised but delivered from brief notes is:
qs.x: Extemporaneous: natural, flexible, keeps eye contact.

qs.q: Which delivery type is best for a press conference or legal statement?
qs.x: Manuscript gives complete accuracy and precise timing.

qs.q: Which type of delivery should you choose to present a science experiment, according to the class question?
qs.x: Well prepared and accurate, with notes for figures, while still keeping eye contact.

qs.q: What are the three stages of preparing an oral presentation?
o: Planning → outlining and structuring → choosing the mode of delivery
qs.x: Planning, then outlining, then the mode of delivery.

qs.q: Which belongs in the conclusion of a presentation?
o: A summary and a vote of thanks
qs.x: The conclusion summarises, re-emphasises, thanks and invites questions.

qs.q: When you don't know the answer to a question after your presentation, you should:
o: admit it and offer to follow up
qs.x: Handle questions gracefully: listen, answer respectfully, admit when you don't know.

qs.q: Too much text on the slides causes:
qs.x: Use short bullets and visuals instead.

qs.q: A student needs the percentage of Batswana aged 18–35 who use the internet. Best source?
qs.x: Numbers come from a statistical report.

qs.q: A research article reporting new findings is a:
qs.x: It reports first-hand, original research.

qs.q: A textbook is usually a:
qs.x: It analyses and interprets others' work.

qs.q: If asked, an encyclopaedia should be called a:
qs.x: It summarises other sources for an overview.

qs.q: Peer review means:
o: experts in the field check an article before it is published
qs.x: Scholarly journals are usually peer-reviewed.

qs.q: Sharing "hot water, honey and garlic cures COVID-19" because you believe it is:
qs.x: Wrong information with no intent to harm.

qs.q: Leaking genuine confidential patient records to cause harm is:
qs.x: Mal = true but malicious.

qs.q: A fake video of a president promoting an investment scam is:
qs.x: Fabricated and meant to harm or scam.

qs.q: In the CRAAP test, the first A stands for:
qs.x: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose.

qs.q: The cumulative record of data from your use of websites, apps and devices is your:
qs.x: It includes data you share and data collected automatically.

qs.q: Reading is a:
qs.x: You take information in; writing is the productive skill.

qs.q: What should decide which reading technique you use?
o: How much time is left in the semester
qs.x: Know why you are reading before you start.

qs.q: Critical reading differs from reading because it:
o: makes judgements by analysing, interpreting and evaluating
only grasps what the text says
qs.x: Critical reading looks at what a text does and means, and links out to other knowledge.

qs.q: Looking quickly for the general idea of a text is:
qs.x: Skimming = gist.

qs.q: Searching the Methods section only for the pH value is:
qs.x: sCanning = speCific detail.

qs.q: Survey → Question → Read → Recite → Review is called:
qs.x: SQ3R is a study-reading method.

qs.q: Breaking a long text into small sections and summarising each in your own words is:
qs.x: Chunking suits long or difficult texts.

qs.q: Highlighting findings, circling unfamiliar terms and writing questions in the margins is:
qs.x: Annotation makes revision easier.

qs.q: Where do you find the meanings of technical terms in a book?
qs.x: Glossary = meanings. Index = where topics are (page numbers).

qs.q: Which feature of a journal article allows survey reading because it summarises the whole paper?
qs.x: The abstract is the summary.

qs.q: Which source is NOT acceptable for academic work?
qs.x: Wikipedia is not reviewed; the others are peer-reviewed or edited.

qs.q: Rewriting one idea in your own words at about the same length is:
qs.x: Change the words and the structure, keep the meaning, and still cite.

qs.q: For a source with three or more authors, the in-text citation uses:
o: the first author only, with no marker
qs.x: e.g. (Naveed et al., 2024).
qs.group: 26. Note making from written sources, citation and referencing

qs.q: Presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own without acknowledging them is:
qs.x: Citation prevents plagiarism and gives credit.
qs.group: 26. Note making from written sources, citation and referencing

qs.q: A student needs the year the Cybercrime Act was passed. She runs her eyes down the page looking only for a date. Which technique?
qs.x: Looking for one specific fact.

qs.q: Before a seminar, a student reads the first and last sentences of each paragraph to get the general idea. Which technique?
qs.x: Reading for the gist.

qs.q: A student previews a chapter's headings, writes questions, reads, summarises the answers in his own words and later reviews his notes. Which technique?
qs.x: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review.

qs.q: While reading, a student highlights the main findings, circles unfamiliar terms and writes questions in the margin. Which technique?
qs.x: Annotation.

qs.q: You need the percentage of Batswana aged 18–35 who use the internet. Most suitable source?
qs.x: Numbers come from statistics.

qs.q: You need a first-hand account from a student who was cyberbullied. Most suitable source?
qs.x: First-hand experience comes from the person.

sets.title: Mock paper: written answers
sets.desc: Write your answer, then tick it against the marking points from the memo.

qs.q: Define proxemics and give two examples of how it can be misinterpreted.
qs.ans:
• Proxemics = the use of space / distance / proximity between people communicating.
  • Names the distances: intimate, personal, social, public (or says distance shows the relationship).
  • Example 1: students sitting very close in a group discussion are thought to be lovers.
  • Example 2: a couple walking apart is thought to have a strained relationship; or a CEO seated far away is read as authoritarian.

qs.q: Define information disorder. Explain what malinformation is and give one example.
qs.ans:
• Information disorder = sharing or developing false (or harmful) information, with or without intent to harm.
  • Malinformation = genuine / true information shared to cause harm.
  • Example: leaking confidential patient records; #GuptaLeaks; WikiLeaks.

qs.q: Define a communication barrier. Explain the barrier of poor encoding and give one example.
qs.ans:
• Barrier = any factor or situation that interferes with / hampers the communication process and stops it succeeding.
  • Poor encoding = the sender fails to put the message in a form the receiver understands: wrong vocabulary, jargon, poor grammar, ambiguity.
  • Example: a lecturer using heavy jargon with first-years; or "If the child does not like the milk, boil it."

qs.q:
The Acid Rain Presentation. Five first-year Chemistry students must present on acid rain on Friday. Their leader, Neo, sends a 900-word WhatsApp message at 2 a.m. on Thursday with the research, slide order, three links and everyone's roles. Most only skim it, and two prepare the same section.

They meet in the library on Thursday afternoon, but a generator runs outside the window and they keep asking each other to repeat themselves. Kagiso explains the chemistry with terms like "dry deposition" and "sulphuric anhydride" without explaining them; the others nod but do not understand.

Lesedi, from a rural village, suggests a local example of crops damaged near Selebi-Phikwe. Boitumelo says, "People from villages don't know about industrial pollution," and the group ignores the idea. Lesedi crosses her arms and stays silent.

Mpho keeps scrolling on his phone and later asks what his part is. Nobody summarises the decisions, and everyone leaves with a different idea of who presents first.

Identify and discuss five communication barriers. For each give the barrier, evidence from the case, its effect and a solution.
qs.ans:
• Information overload / poor timing: 900 words at 2 a.m. → skimmed, duplicated work. Fix: short message at a sensible time, confirm roles.
  • Physical noise: generator outside → couldn't hear. Fix: quiet room, close the window.
  • Poor encoding (jargon): Kagiso's unexplained terms → no understanding; nodding was false feedback. Fix: simple language, check understanding.
  • Stereotyping / attitude: "People from villages…" → good idea ignored, Lesedi withdrew. Fix: judge ideas on merit, cultural sensitivity.
  • NVC: crossed arms and silence → hurt or disagreement, her input lost. Fix: the leader notices and invites her to speak.
  • Marginal attention: Mpho on his phone → missed his role. Fix: phones away, active listening.
  • Lack of feedback / no summary → different ideas of the order. Fix: summarise and confirm decisions in writing.
  • Any 5 of these 7: 1 mark for the barrier with evidence, 1 for the effect AND a solution.

qs.q: Distinguish between listening and hearing.
qs.ans:
• Listening = active: hearing with a purpose, with concentration, interpretation, understanding and action.
  • Hearing = passive: just receiving sound.

qs.q: Distinguish between skimming and scanning.
qs.ans:
• Skimming = reading quickly for the general idea / gist (topic and last sentences).
  • Scanning = moving the eyes quickly to find specific information (a date, figure, name).

qs.q: Distinguish between primary and secondary sources.
qs.ans:
• Primary = original, first-hand evidence, e.g. a research article, diary, interview, an Act.
  • Secondary = by someone who did not experience it; analyses or interprets primary sources, e.g. a textbook.

qs.q: Distinguish between note-taking and note-making.
qs.ans:
• Note-taking = notes from oral sources (lectures, tutorials), usually in real time.
  • Note-making = notes from written sources, at your own pace, with paraphrasing, summarising and citation.

qs.q:
"Good afternoon, everyone. Today I am going to talk about pollution in Gaborone Dam. First, let us look at the causes. Most pollution comes from sewage and farm chemicals. However, litter from nearby residents is also a serious problem. Now let's move on to the effects. Fish die because oxygen levels drop; therefore, local fishermen lose income. In addition, the water becomes unsafe to drink. The key point to remember is that most of this pollution is caused by people. To sum up, pollution in the dam is human-made and harmful, so everyone must play a part in protecting it."

Identify three signposts and three discourse markers from the speech, and state the function of each.
qs.ans:
• Signposts: "Today I am going to talk about…" (introduces the topic) · "First, let us look at…" (first point) · "Now let's move on to…" (transition) · "The key point to remember is…" (important information) · "To sum up…" (conclusion).
  • Discourse markers: "However" (contrast) · "because" (cause) · "therefore" (result) · "In addition" (adding) · "so" (consequence).
  • "First" counts as either, but not in both lists. Any 3 + 3, 1 mark each.
